roles.label: Finance & Accounting

situations.label: Month-end close

situations.label: Variance review
situations.description: Explain performance differences and distinguish timing from structural drivers.

situations.label: Budget and forecast
situations.description: Test assumptions and communicate the likely financial outlook.

situations.label: Audit discussion
situations.description: Provide evidence and explain judgements to an internal or external reviewer.

roles.label: Project & Product Management
roles.description: Setting priorities, managing delivery choices, and keeping stakeholders aligned on outcomes.

situations.label: Roadmap prioritisation
situations.description: Compare opportunities and decide what should be delivered first.

situations.label: Scope change
situations.description: Assess a requested change and agree its effect on time, cost, or quality.

situations.label: Stakeholder update
situations.description: Summarise progress, risks, decisions, and the next milestone.

situations.label: Delivery retrospective
situations.description: Learn from delivery without reducing the discussion to blame.

roles.label: Technology & Engineering
roles.description: Explaining technical choices, managing operational risk, and collaborating on robust systems.

situations.label: Architecture review
situations.description: Evaluate a design against constraints, failure modes, and future needs.

situations.label: Incident response
situations.description: Coordinate recovery and communicate impact under pressure.

situations.label: Code review
situations.description: Improve a change through specific, respectful technical feedback.

situations.label: Technical interview
situations.description: Explain an approach, test assumptions, and reason aloud.

roles.label: Sales & Business Development
roles.description: Discovering customer needs, communicating value, and progressing commercial relationships.

situations.label: Discovery call
situations.description: Understand the customer’s problem, urgency, and decision process.

situations.label: Proposal pitch
situations.description: Connect an offer to measurable customer value.

situations.label: Objection handling
situations.description: Address concern without becoming defensive or dismissive.

situations.label: Pipeline review
situations.description: Assess opportunity quality and agree the next commercial action.

roles.label: HR & People Leadership

situations.label: Performance conversation
situations.description: Discuss expectations, evidence, and improvement respectfully.

situations.label: Hiring interview
situations.description: Assess capability consistently while giving the candidate a fair experience.

situations.label: Team conflict
situations.description: Surface different perspectives and restore a workable relationship.

situations.label: Organisational change
situations.description: Explain change honestly and help people understand what follows.

roles.label: Consulting & Strategy

situations.label: Problem framing
situations.description: Turn an ambiguous concern into a focused question and testable structure.

situations.label: Client readout
situations.description: Present evidence, implications, and outstanding questions succinctly.

situations.label: Executive recommendation
situations.description: Make a concise, evidence-based case for action.

situations.label: Workshop facilitation
situations.description: Guide a group towards shared insight and concrete decisions.

roles.label: Operations & Supply Chain
roles.description: Maintaining flow, improving reliability, and coordinating practical responses to disruption.

situations.label: Capacity planning

situations.label: Supplier negotiation
situations.description: Agree commercial and service conditions while protecting continuity.

situations.label: Process improvement
situations.description: Diagnose wasted effort and establish a more reliable flow.

situations.label: Disruption response
situations.description: Protect essential service and coordinate recovery from an interruption.

situations.label: Consent discussion

situations.label: Service escalation

seniorityLevels.label: Early career
seniorityLevels.description: Building confidence in routine professional conversations and written updates.
seniorityLevels.communicationFocus: State the situation clearly, ask focused questions, and confirm the next action.

seniorityLevels.label: Experienced contributor
seniorityLevels.description: Owning specialised work and influencing colleagues without relying on formal authority.
seniorityLevels.communicationFocus: Explain reasoning, surface trade-offs, and offer a practical recommendation.

seniorityLevels.label: Manager

seniorityLevels.communicationFocus: Create alignment, give specific feedback, and make ownership unmistakable.

seniorityLevels.label: Senior leader

seniorityLevels.communicationFocus: Frame the wider context, acknowledge risk, and set a clear direction.

seniorityLevels.label: Executive

seniorityLevels.communicationFocus: Be concise, commercially grounded, and explicit about the decision required.

goals.label: Clarify a complex point
goals.outcome: The listener understands the issue, evidence, and implication without unnecessary detail.
goals.coachingPrompt: What is the one distinction your listener must understand?

goals.label: Build alignment
goals.outcome: People leave with a shared interpretation of the priority, ownership, and next step.
goals.coachingPrompt: Which assumption or responsibility needs to become explicit?

goals.label: Influence a decision
goals.outcome: A recommendation feels credible, relevant, and easy to act on.
goals.coachingPrompt: What matters most to the decision-maker, and what evidence supports your case?

goals.label: Make a recommendation
goals.outcome: The preferred course of action and its rationale are both unmistakable.
goals.coachingPrompt: Can you state your recommendation before explaining the supporting detail?

goals.label: Negotiate constructively
goals.outcome: Interests and constraints are explored without making the conversation adversarial.
goals.coachingPrompt: Which condition is essential, and where can you offer flexibility?

goals.label: Challenge diplomatically
goals.outcome: A weak assumption or risky choice is questioned while trust remains intact.
goals.coachingPrompt: How can you challenge the idea without assigning blame to the person?

goals.label: Coach for improvement
goals.outcome: Feedback is specific, fair, and connected to an achievable next behaviour.
goals.coachingPrompt: What observable behaviour should continue or change next time?

goals.label: Reassure with honesty
goals.outcome: Concern is acknowledged and confidence is supported without minimising real risk.
goals.coachingPrompt: What is known, what remains uncertain, and what is being done now?

words.meaning: A difference between figures, records, or statements that were expected to agree.
words.example: We found a £240 discrepancy between the travel summary and the supporting report.
words.whenToUse: Use it to name a specific mismatch before you know or explain its cause.
words.avoidOrMisuse: A discrepancy is a difference to investigate; it does not by itself establish fraud or an error in either source.
words.mission: Describe a discrepancy between two fictional reports and say what you would compare next.

sales-business-development.meaning: A difference between two figures, statements, or records that should be checked to understand whether they are consistent.
sales-business-development.example: There is a discrepancy between the user count in the quotation and the number agreed during our latest discovery call.
sales-business-development.whenToUse: Use when pointing out a specific inconsistency without prematurely deciding whether it reflects an error or a changed assumption.
sales-business-development.avoidOrMisuse: Do not treat every discrepancy as misconduct; identify the two sources and ask which information should guide the revision.
sales-business-development.mission: Raise a fictional discrepancy between a proposal and a meeting note, then suggest a straightforward method for checking and correcting the record.

operations-supply-chain.meaning: A difference between records, accounts, or observations that should be consistent and therefore needs explanation.
operations-supply-chain.example: We found a discrepancy of two cartons between the receipt and the bay count, but the inspection-area check remains open.
operations-supply-chain.whenToUse: Use it to flag a factual inconsistency while keeping the explanation open until the relevant evidence has been checked.
operations-supply-chain.avoidOrMisuse: A discrepancy is not proof of theft, negligence, or a physical shortage; name the compared sources without assigning unsupported blame.
operations-supply-chain.mission: Report a fictional receipt discrepancy neutrally, quantify the difference, and request the next check needed to explain it.

people-human-resources.meaning: A difference between accounts, records, or expectations that needs clarification before people draw a confident conclusion.
people-human-resources.example: There is a discrepancy between the meeting note and the manager's recollection of the deadline, so we should check what was communicated.
people-human-resources.whenToUse: Use when identifying an inconsistency neutrally without assuming dishonesty, fault, or a particular explanation for the difference.
people-human-resources.avoidOrMisuse: A discrepancy is not proof that either person is deliberately misleading others; name the sources and ask how the difference arose.
people-human-resources.mission: Raise a fictional discrepancy between two accounts of an assignment and propose a neutral question that could clarify the original agreement.

healthcare.meaning: An inconsistency between pieces of information that would normally be expected to agree.
healthcare.example: There is a discrepancy between the meeting room on the appointment letter and the room recorded on the approved clinic schedule.
healthcare.whenToUse: Use it to describe conflicting records neutrally while asking for the appropriate verification or correction.
healthcare.avoidOrMisuse: A discrepancy is not proof of negligence or permission to select the version you prefer; use the authorised reconciliation process.
healthcare.mission: Report a fictional appointment-record discrepancy, naming both sources and requesting confirmation without assigning blame or changing the record yourself.

consulting-strategy.meaning: A difference between figures, accounts, or records that calls for explanation before they can be treated as consistent evidence.
consulting-strategy.example: There is a discrepancy between the reported completion date and the system record, so we should clarify what each source counts as completion.
consulting-strategy.whenToUse: Use when drawing attention to a specific difference without deciding prematurely whether it is an error or a valid definitional distinction.
consulting-strategy.avoidOrMisuse: Do not assume a discrepancy indicates deliberate misrepresentation; name the sources and the exact information that differs.
consulting-strategy.mission: Raise a fictional discrepancy in a client dataset and propose a neutral way to check the definitions before revising the finding.

words.meaning: Not yet completed, settled, or resolved at the time being discussed.
words.example: Two supplier confirmations remain outstanding, and each has a named follow-up owner.
words.whenToUse: Use it in a status update to distinguish open work or unpaid amounts from completed items.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Outstanding can also mean excellent; specify an item, balance, or action to make the intended meaning clear.
words.mission: Name one outstanding close action, its owner, and the expected update time.

words.meaning: The agreed boundary or time used to decide which items belong in a reporting period or submission.
words.example: Please confirm the reporting cut-off before sending the final list of June deliveries.
words.whenToUse: Use it when a deadline or period boundary affects the completeness and timing of a report.
words.avoidOrMisuse: A submission deadline and an accounting period boundary may differ; state which cut-off you mean.
words.mission: Write a message asking a colleague to confirm the cut-off relevant to a fictional report.

words.meaning: To assign an amount, resource, or share to a particular purpose, team, or category.
words.example: We will allocate the shared training cost using the department split already agreed with the team.
words.whenToUse: Use it when explaining where a cost or resource is assigned and the basis for that assignment.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Allocating a cost is not the same as paying it; explain the assignment basis rather than implying a cash movement.
words.mission: Explain how you would allocate a fictional shared cost using a stated, agreed basis.

words.meaning: To combine separate inputs into a single organised view or report.
words.example: I will consolidate the branch updates into one close-status report for the controller.
words.whenToUse: Use it to explain that several inputs will be brought together in a coherent view.
words.avoidOrMisuse: In formal group accounting, consolidation has a specific technical meaning; describe the actual process rather than implying that combining spreadsheets completes it.
words.mission: Say which three inputs you will consolidate and who will use the combined report.

operations-supply-chain.meaning: To combine separate operational items or activities into a coordinated group, often to improve handling or resource use.
operations-supply-chain.example: We can consolidate the three late orders into one collection if their destination route, handling requirements, and customer timing are compatible.
operations-supply-chain.whenToUse: Use it when combining loads, work, or records may reduce duplication while still meeting the relevant service conditions.
operations-supply-chain.avoidOrMisuse: Consolidation can delay an urgent item while others become ready; check compatibility and timing rather than assuming fewer movements are always better.
operations-supply-chain.mission: Recommend whether to consolidate fictional deliveries, identifying the benefit and a condition favouring separate collections.

words.meaning: A change made to a figure, entry, or plan to reflect additional information or correct a problem.
words.example: The adjustment removes a duplicated travel line from the department's draft report.
words.whenToUse: Use it when explaining what changed, why it changed, and whether approval is still needed.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Do not call an unexplained difference an adjustment; identify the actual change and its reason.
words.mission: Describe a fictional report adjustment and explain the before-and-after effect.

words.meaning: The extent to which all the information or items required for a defined purpose are included.
words.example: Our completeness check compares the submitted files with the agreed list of department reports.
words.whenToUse: Use it when the question is whether required information is missing.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Completeness does not establish accuracy; a report can include every required item and still contain wrong figures.
words.mission: Describe how you would check the completeness of a fictional close submission.

words.meaning: Available for use for now but still subject to confirmation or change.
words.example: The £18,000 estimate is provisional until the supplier confirms the remaining work.
words.whenToUse: Use it to share useful working information while signalling what still needs confirmation.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Provisional does not mean careless; state the reason it may change and what will resolve the uncertainty.
words.mission: Present a provisional figure and name the information needed to confirm it.

project-product.meaning: Arranged or proposed for now but subject to confirmation or change when more information becomes available.
project-product.example: June remains the provisional launch month until the supplier confirms its integration requirements.
project-product.whenToUse: Use it when stakeholders need a working plan before the conditions for a firm commitment are satisfied.
project-product.avoidOrMisuse: Do not leave a provisional date indefinitely unresolved; give the confirmation condition and next review point.
project-product.mission: Communicate a provisional delivery date together with the evidence needed to confirm or revise it.

sales-business-development.meaning: Agreed or suggested for the moment but still open to confirmation or change when relevant information becomes available.
sales-business-development.example: We have reserved a provisional training date, which we can confirm once your team approves the number of participants.
sales-business-development.whenToUse: Use when distinguishing a working arrangement from a final commitment and identifying what remains to be settled.
sales-business-development.avoidOrMisuse: Do not rely on provisional alone to explain uncertainty; state what could change and who will provide confirmation.
sales-business-development.mission: Clarify a fictional provisional launch date in a customer email, including the outstanding dependency and when you expect to revisit it.

operations-supply-chain.meaning: Tentative and usable for now, but subject to confirmation, revision, or approval when further evidence becomes available.
operations-supply-chain.example: Our provisional conclusion is that the briefing helped reduce errors, pending a comparison of returns with similar product complexity.
operations-supply-chain.whenToUse: Use it to mark a working operational interpretation or arrangement that colleagues may use within clearly stated limits.
operations-supply-chain.avoidOrMisuse: Do not use provisional as a permanent escape from commitment; say what will confirm the position and when it will be reviewed.
operations-supply-chain.mission: Give a fictional provisional conclusion about a returns trial and identify the missing evidence and the planned review point.

people-human-resources.meaning: Held or proposed for the moment while remaining open to revision as further relevant information becomes available.
people-human-resources.example: Our provisional interpretation is that role boundaries are unclear, and we will revisit it after discussing examples with both affected teams.
people-human-resources.whenToUse: Use when sharing a working interpretation or recommendation that helps progress but should not be mistaken for a final judgement.
people-human-resources.avoidOrMisuse: Say what could change the provisional view; avoid using the word merely to protect a conclusion you have no intention of revisiting.
people-human-resources.mission: Offer a fictional provisional interpretation of a team issue and state which additional evidence would make you revise it.

healthcare.meaning: Tentative and subject to confirmation or change before it can be treated as settled.
healthcare.example: The interpreter arrangement remains provisional until the approved booking service confirms the request and the coordinator records that response.
healthcare.whenToUse: Use it when a communication or service arrangement is being considered but has not yet received required confirmation.
healthcare.avoidOrMisuse: Patients may hear a tentative arrangement as a promise; state the condition clearly and identify who will provide the next update.
healthcare.mission: Explain a fictional provisional appointment-support arrangement in plain English, including the missing confirmation and the responsible contact.

words.meaning: To complete the remaining changes or checks so that a document or arrangement is ready for its intended use.
words.example: We can finalise the report once the two department owners confirm their updates.
words.whenToUse: Use it to explain the last steps before a report or agreement is considered complete.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Finalising a document does not necessarily mean it has been formally approved; keep completion and approval distinct.
words.mission: Say what must happen before you can finalise a fictional finance report.

words.meaning: Formal confirmation that the appropriate person has reviewed and approved a specified item.
words.example: The pack is ready for sign-off from the controller after the remaining query is answered.
words.whenToUse: Use it when approval must be distinguished from preparation or informal agreement.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Do not imply that sign-off covers work outside the stated review; identify the item and the authorised reviewer.
words.mission: Request sign-off for a fictional report and state exactly what the reviewer is approving.

words.meaning: Able to be followed back to its source or through the steps that produced it.
words.example: Each total in the summary is traceable to a dated department file and a calculation tab.
words.whenToUse: Use it when another person needs to understand where a figure came from or how it changed.
words.avoidOrMisuse: A traceable figure is not automatically correct; traceability makes the source and process easier to check.
words.mission: Explain how a fictional report total is traceable to its supporting information.

words.meaning: Following the same stated approach or remaining in agreement across comparable items.
words.example: Please use consistent department names so readers can compare the monthly reports.
words.whenToUse: Use it when comparable reports need a shared definition, format, or treatment.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Consistency alone does not show that an approach is appropriate; explain any necessary change rather than preserving a known problem.
words.mission: Ask a colleague to use a consistent definition and explain why the comparison needs it.

people-human-resources.meaning: Following a coherent approach or standard across comparable situations, while making any relevant differences in treatment explicit.
people-human-resources.example: We need a consistent approach to feedback: describe the behaviour, explain its effect, and invite the colleague's perspective before discussing improvements.
people-human-resources.whenToUse: Use when helping managers apply a shared communication process or clarify the standard used to discuss comparable work.
people-human-resources.avoidOrMisuse: Consistent does not always mean identical; explain the common principle and acknowledge relevant differences in context rather than ignoring them.
people-human-resources.mission: Describe a fictional consistent approach to project feedback, then explain how you would adapt the conversation to a colleague's particular circumstances.

words.meaning: The transfer of work, information, and responsibility from one person or team to another.
words.example: The handover note lists the open queries, their owners, and the links to supporting files.
words.whenToUse: Use it when a colleague must continue your work without guessing what remains to be done.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Sending a folder is not a complete handover if the recipient cannot identify the status, owner, and next action.
words.mission: Write a handover sentence that names one open item, its status, and its next owner.

operations-supply-chain.meaning: A structured transfer of operational information and responsibility between people or shifts so unfinished work can continue coherently.
operations-supply-chain.example: The evening handover identifies the unresolved scanner check, the orders it affects, and the colleague responsible for the next update.
operations-supply-chain.whenToUse: Use it at shift changes or task transfers when the receiving person needs context, pending actions, and clear responsibility.
operations-supply-chain.avoidOrMisuse: Sending a note does not prove the receiving shift understands it; allow questions and confirm acceptance of outstanding actions.
operations-supply-chain.mission: Deliver a fictional warehouse handover containing one completed action, one pending check, its owner, and its next update time.

people-human-resources.meaning: The transfer of relevant work, information, and responsibility from one person or team to another.
people-human-resources.example: The handover should explain the open client questions and current deadlines so the incoming colleague can identify what needs attention first.
people-human-resources.whenToUse: Use when discussing how people gain the context needed to take over work without avoidable confusion or missing information.
people-human-resources.avoidOrMisuse: A handover is not complete merely because files were sent; check understanding and distinguish transferred information from agreed responsibility.
people-human-resources.mission: Outline a fictional handover conversation with the current status, an unresolved issue, and a question that checks the recipient's understanding.

healthcare.meaning: A structured transfer of relevant information and responsibility between professionals or teams during a change of care responsibility.
healthcare.example: The handover identifies the requested accessible plan, the pending delivery check, and the colleague accepting that follow-up responsibility.
healthcare.whenToUse: Use it when a receiving team needs context, outstanding actions, and an opportunity to clarify responsibility.
healthcare.avoidOrMisuse: Sending a record alone does not confirm understanding or acceptance; follow the organisation's approved handover arrangements and responsibility rules.
healthcare.mission: Practise a fictional handover of an appointment-information request, naming the pending action and asking the receiving colleague to confirm responsibility.

words.meaning: A factor that causes or substantially influences a result or change.
words.example: Higher shipment volumes were the main driver of the increase in packaging costs.
words.whenToUse: Use it to connect a reported movement to the factor that explains it.
words.avoidOrMisuse: A movement in another figure is not automatically a driver; show the relationship rather than assuming causation.
words.mission: Identify the main driver of a fictional cost increase and name supporting information.

words.meaning: Able to be explained as resulting from a particular cause or source.
words.example: About £6,000 of the increase is attributable to the extra customer event confirmed in the schedule.
words.whenToUse: Use it to state the part of a result that a supported cause explains.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Use attributable to, not attributable for, and avoid claiming a cause is proven when it is only suspected.
words.mission: Explain how much of a fictional variance is attributable to a documented event.

words.meaning: Happening repeatedly or expected to return at intervals.
words.example: The new monthly support fee is a recurring cost in the team's operating plan.
words.whenToUse: Use it when repetition affects the explanation or the expected future result.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Recurring does not mean guaranteed or permanent; state the period and any known end date.
words.mission: Identify a recurring cost and explain its effect on the next forecast.

words.meaning: Unusual compared with the normal pattern being discussed.
words.example: The office relocation was an exceptional event in the department's monthly spending pattern.
words.whenToUse: Use it to explain why a specific event differs from ordinary activity.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Calling an event exceptional in conversation does not establish a formal accounting classification or mean it can be ignored.
words.mission: Describe an exceptional event and explain why it differs from normal activity.

words.meaning: An amount or effect that partly or fully balances an opposite amount or effect.
words.example: Lower travel spending provides a partial offset to the higher training cost.
words.whenToUse: Use it to explain opposing movements before stating their combined effect.
words.avoidOrMisuse: An offset may be only partial; state the amounts rather than implying that the whole impact disappears.
words.mission: Describe an offset between two fictional cost movements and state the net change.

words.meaning: Similar enough in relevant definitions and circumstances to support a useful comparison.
words.example: The two branches are not directly comparable because one handles substantially more complex orders.
words.whenToUse: Use it before interpreting differences between periods, teams, or external reference points.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Comparable does not mean identical; identify the important differences that remain.
words.mission: Explain whether two fictional teams' costs are comparable and give one reason.

words.meaning: Describing the more basic condition or pattern beneath a visible result.
words.example: After separating the delivery-date shift, the underlying demand trend appears stable.
words.whenToUse: Use it when looking beyond a temporary or surface movement to a supported broader pattern.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Explain what you have separated or adjusted; underlying is not permission to remove inconvenient results.
words.mission: Describe an underlying trend and distinguish it from one temporary effect.

words.meaning: To express the size or extent of something in numbers.
words.example: Please quantify the impact of the delayed shipment on next month's expected receipts.
words.whenToUse: Use it when a qualitative statement needs an amount, percentage, count, or defined range.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Numbers are not automatically precise; state the units, period, and uncertainty behind an estimate.
words.mission: Ask a colleague to quantify a fictional delay's impact, specifying the period and units.

sales-business-development.meaning: Express an amount, effect, or difference using numbers, with a clear method and an appropriate level of precision.
sales-business-development.example: We can quantify the current reporting effort by asking the trial team to record time spent on the same tasks for one week.
sales-business-development.whenToUse: Use when turning a broad value claim into something measurable that the customer can inspect and discuss.
sales-business-development.avoidOrMisuse: Do not invent precise numbers for uncertain benefits; explain how the measurement was obtained and which important effects it excludes.
sales-business-development.mission: Suggest a practical way to quantify a fictional customer's current manual work, stating the measure, observation period, and one limitation.

consulting-strategy.meaning: Express the size, amount, or effect of something using numbers and a clear account of the measurement or estimation method.
consulting-strategy.example: We can quantify the observed rework hours, but translating them into future savings requires assumptions about how much of the work the redesign will remove.
consulting-strategy.whenToUse: Use when making the scale of a problem or proposal more concrete while distinguishing measurements from estimates.
consulting-strategy.avoidOrMisuse: Do not imply false precision or assume every important consequence is numerical; explain the method, uncertainty, and effects left outside the estimate.
consulting-strategy.mission: Quantify a fictional process issue using a simple stated measure, then explain which part of the proposed benefit remains an estimate.

words.meaning: Appropriate in scale to the size, significance, or risk of the issue.
words.example: A targeted review of the affected invoices would be proportionate to the issue identified.
words.whenToUse: Use it when explaining why a proposed response has the right scale for the problem.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Proportionate does not simply mean smaller or cheaper; connect the response to the issue's significance.
words.mission: Recommend a proportionate response to a fictional reporting query and explain the scale.

operations-supply-chain.meaning: Appropriate in scale and intensity to the evidenced issue, likely impact, and relevant operational requirements.
operations-supply-chain.example: A proportionate response would consider the confirmed lane-one fault separately from the other lanes that passed the agreed equipment checks.
operations-supply-chain.whenToUse: Use it when testing whether a proposed restriction, investigation, or resource commitment matches the actual operational circumstances.
operations-supply-chain.avoidOrMisuse: Proportionate does not mean the cheapest or least disruptive option; required safety, quality, and contractual controls cannot simply be waived.
operations-supply-chain.mission: Question a fictional proposal to stop every dispatch lane, requesting evidence on scope while preserving required checks and decision authority.

people-human-resources.meaning: Appropriate in scale or intensity to the issue, evidence, and context being considered rather than excessive or insufficient.
people-human-resources.example: A proportionate next step is to clarify the missed handoff and agree an update practice, rather than drawing a sweeping conclusion about the person's character.
people-human-resources.whenToUse: Use when discussing a communication response that fits what is currently known, without making formal policy or disciplinary determinations.
people-human-resources.avoidOrMisuse: Explain the relationship between the concern and the response; proportionate is a judgement requiring context, not a universal rule.
people-human-resources.mission: Recommend a proportionate communication response to a fictional one-off misunderstanding, stating what remains unknown and why your proposed discussion fits the evidence.

healthcare.meaning: Appropriate in scale to the identified issue, its implications, and the requirements that must still be met.
healthcare.example: A proportionate improvement is to verify and label the contact numbers before proposing a full redesign of the appointment service.
healthcare.whenToUse: Use it when matching a communication intervention to a clearly defined problem while preserving required safeguards.
healthcare.avoidOrMisuse: Proportionate does not mean ignoring safety, accessibility, or privacy obligations; any clinical implications require qualified review under local procedures.
healthcare.mission: Explain why a fictional letter revision is a proportionate response to confusing contact information and identify the approval it still needs.

words.meaning: Better than the stated comparison or beneficial from the specified point of view.
words.example: The cost movement is favourable against plan, although part of it reflects work delayed until next month.
words.whenToUse: Use it when describing a result relative to a clearly identified objective or comparison.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Lower spending is not always good overall; mention delayed work, reduced output, or other relevant consequences.
words.mission: Explain a favourable cost movement and one qualification that a manager should understand.

words.meaning: Unhelpful, harmful, or worse than the stated comparison.
words.example: The adverse revenue movement against plan is mainly explained by a later delivery date.
words.whenToUse: Use it to state a negative direction calmly before explaining the cause and response.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Adverse describes an effect or comparison, not a person's motives; do not use it as a substitute for evidence.
words.mission: Describe an adverse movement and separate its cause from the proposed response.

words.meaning: An explanation that helps a reader interpret figures, events, or results.
words.example: The variance commentary explains the timing change rather than simply repeating the table.
words.whenToUse: Use it for the written explanation accompanying a report or presentation of numbers.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Commentary should add causes, implications, or qualifications; restating every figure does not explain the result.
words.mission: Write two sentences of commentary explaining a fictional result and its main implication.

words.meaning: Something treated as true for the purpose of planning or analysis, although it may need confirmation.
words.example: Our forecast uses the assumption that the supplier can deliver the equipment in November.
words.whenToUse: Use it to make the conditions behind an estimate or recommendation visible.
words.avoidOrMisuse: An assumption is not a confirmed fact; explain its basis and what would cause you to revisit it.
words.mission: State one assumption behind a fictional forecast and how you would check it.

project-product.meaning: Something treated as true for planning or reasoning even though it has not yet been fully confirmed.
project-product.example: Our estimate uses the assumption that the supplier's interface requires no additional approval process.
project-product.whenToUse: Use it to reveal the conditions underlying an estimate, business case, or delivery plan.
project-product.avoidOrMisuse: Do not hide a critical assumption in a footnote while presenting the resulting date as unconditional.
project-product.mission: State the supplier assumption behind the June forecast and explain how you will verify it.

sales-business-development.meaning: Something treated as true for an estimate or proposal even though it has not yet been fully established.
sales-business-development.example: Our estimate rests on the assumption that all five branches will start using the service during the first month.
sales-business-development.whenToUse: Use when making the basis of a sales estimate transparent and inviting the customer or colleagues to verify it.
sales-business-development.avoidOrMisuse: Do not hide an assumption inside a confident statement of fact; explain how a different answer could change the proposal.
sales-business-development.mission: State one assumption behind a fictional savings estimate, ask the buyer to verify it, and describe what you would revise if it proved wrong.

operations-supply-chain.meaning: A condition treated as true for planning or reasoning even though it may not yet be confirmed.
operations-supply-chain.example: Our planning assumption is that promotional orders rise by 15 percent, but sales has not yet confirmed the campaign's launch date.
operations-supply-chain.whenToUse: Use it to make uncertain inputs visible before stakeholders rely on a forecast, delivery promise, or resource request.
operations-supply-chain.avoidOrMisuse: Do not bury material assumptions in supporting notes or describe them as verified facts; state who will validate them and when.
operations-supply-chain.mission: State a fictional seasonal staffing assumption and ask the relevant team to confirm or revise it.

healthcare.meaning: Something treated as true in reasoning despite not having been established by the available information.
healthcare.example: It is an assumption that the patient declined the discussion simply because the portal message has no recorded reply.
healthcare.whenToUse: Use it when an interpretation of communication behaviour is being mistaken for an established fact.
healthcare.avoidOrMisuse: Do not replace one unsupported assumption with another; identify what the record actually shows and what should be checked.
healthcare.mission: Identify an assumption in a fictional non-response note and rewrite the update using only the recorded contact facts.

consulting-strategy.meaning: Something treated as true for the purpose of analysis or planning even though it has not yet been fully established.
consulting-strategy.example: The estimate uses the assumption that demand remains close to the current level while the new handoff process is introduced.
consulting-strategy.whenToUse: Use when making the analytical basis of a recommendation explicit and identifying what should be checked before relying on the result.
consulting-strategy.avoidOrMisuse: Do not bury a decision-sensitive assumption in supporting detail; explain how a different value or answer could change the conclusion.
consulting-strategy.mission: State a fictional assumption behind a recommendation and ask the client for the information needed to test whether it is reasonable.

words.meaning: An agreed starting position used as a reference for measuring change.
words.example: The approved March plan remains the baseline for explaining subsequent changes.
words.whenToUse: Use it when readers need to know the exact starting point behind a comparison.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Do not silently change the baseline between comparisons; name its date and version.
words.mission: Identify the baseline for a fictional comparison and explain why its version matters.

project-product.meaning: A defined starting measurement or reference position against which later performance or change can be compared.
project-product.example: The baseline is twenty clarification calls per thousand cancellation-page visits during the previous four weeks.
project-product.whenToUse: Use it when reporting improvement requires a comparable picture of the position before intervention.
project-product.avoidOrMisuse: Do not compare a holiday-period baseline with an ordinary week without considering differences in customer behaviour.
project-product.mission: Define a baseline for the wording test and name one factor that could make the comparison misleading.

operations-supply-chain.meaning: An explicitly chosen starting measure used to assess later operational changes under reasonably comparable conditions.
operations-supply-chain.example: We used the previous four stable weeks as the packing baseline, excluding the documented period when the line was being installed.
operations-supply-chain.whenToUse: Use it before a process trial so colleagues understand the reference point against which improvement will be evaluated.
operations-supply-chain.avoidOrMisuse: A convenient low-performing week can exaggerate gains; disclose the period, conditions, exclusions, and reason for choosing your baseline.
operations-supply-chain.mission: Define a defensible baseline for a fictional packing trial and explain one condition needed for a fair comparison.

people-human-resources.meaning: An initial or reference measure used as a stated point of comparison for later observations or change.
people-human-resources.example: We will use the first completed month as a baseline and check whether later results use the same question and participant group.
people-human-resources.whenToUse: Use when making clear what a future comparison will be measured against and whether the measures are comparable.
people-human-resources.avoidOrMisuse: Do not call any earlier number a valid baseline without checking its definition, collection method, and relevance to the later result.
people-human-resources.mission: Propose a fictional baseline for reviewing a new team communication practice and explain the conditions needed for a fair later comparison.

consulting-strategy.meaning: A stated reference measure or starting condition against which later results, differences, or proposed changes are compared.
consulting-strategy.example: The baseline uses the six weeks before the process change, and the later comparison should apply the same waiting-time definition and opening hours.
consulting-strategy.whenToUse: Use when explaining where an improvement estimate starts and what must remain comparable for the difference to be meaningful.
consulting-strategy.avoidOrMisuse: An earlier figure is not automatically an appropriate baseline; check definitions, unusual events, and differences in the population being measured.
consulting-strategy.mission: Define a fictional baseline for a service improvement review and identify one condition you would check before comparing it with later performance.

words.meaning: An estimate of a future result based on current information and stated assumptions.
words.example: The updated forecast reflects the delivery dates confirmed by the operations team this week.
words.whenToUse: Use it when communicating the expected future position and why that expectation changed.
words.avoidOrMisuse: A forecast is neither a guaranteed outcome nor automatically the same as a target or approved budget.
words.mission: Present a fictional forecast update and name the new information behind it.

words.meaning: Related to a pattern that tends to recur at particular times of the year.
words.example: The team expects a seasonal peak in support requests during the summer registration period.
words.whenToUse: Use it when a recurring annual pattern helps explain the timing or size of activity.
words.avoidOrMisuse: A single rise in summer does not establish a seasonal pattern; explain the evidence for repetition.
words.mission: Describe a seasonal pattern and how it changes the interpretation of a monthly result.

words.meaning: The direction and pattern in which a measure develops over time.
words.example: The cost trajectory flattens after September as the temporary project team reduces in size.
words.whenToUse: Use it to discuss the direction of several periods rather than one isolated figure.
words.avoidOrMisuse: A trajectory is not a promise; explain whether it is observed, expected, or a target.
words.mission: Describe a fictional cost trajectory and identify what could change its direction.

words.meaning: The degree to which a result changes when an input or assumption changes.
words.example: We will test the sensitivity of expected receipts to a one-week change in delivery timing.
words.whenToUse: Use it when explaining which assumptions have a large or small effect on a projection.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Sensitivity describes how results respond; it does not tell you how likely the changed assumption is.
words.mission: Explain which input you would vary to test the sensitivity of a fictional forecast.

sales-business-development.meaning: The extent to which an estimate or outcome changes when a particular input or assumption changes.
sales-business-development.example: The savings estimate has high sensitivity to transaction volume, so we should test it using the customer's quieter months as well.
sales-business-development.whenToUse: Use when explaining why a commercial calculation may change significantly under different prices, volumes, or implementation conditions.
sales-business-development.avoidOrMisuse: Specify what is sensitive to what; avoid implying that a sensitivity calculation proves which future outcome is most likely.
sales-business-development.mission: Explain which input most affects a fictional value estimate and compare how the conclusion changes under a lower and a higher input.

operations-supply-chain.meaning: The extent to which an operational result or recommendation changes when an input assumption changes.
operations-supply-chain.example: The sensitivity analysis shows how planned overtime changes when weekly orders rise or fall around the current promotion assumption.
operations-supply-chain.whenToUse: Use it to reveal which assumptions materially influence a capacity decision and where further information would be valuable.
operations-supply-chain.avoidOrMisuse: Changing one input is not a complete scenario analysis; specify what varied, what stayed fixed, and the range examined.
operations-supply-chain.mission: Explain a fictional staffing plan's sensitivity to order volume and identify the input you would verify before approving overtime.

consulting-strategy.meaning: The extent to which an analytical result changes when an input, assumption, or condition changes.
consulting-strategy.example: The estimate has high sensitivity to demand because the proposed team can absorb modest growth but would need additional capacity beyond that point.
consulting-strategy.whenToUse: Use when explaining which assumptions matter most to a recommendation and where further evidence or planning deserves attention.
consulting-strategy.avoidOrMisuse: Sensitivity does not tell you which input value will occur; separate testing a result's response from predicting future conditions.
consulting-strategy.mission: Explain a fictional recommendation's sensitivity to one important assumption, comparing what changes under a lower and a higher value.

words.meaning: A defined set of possible conditions used to explore what could happen.
words.example: In the later-delivery scenario, part of the expected cash receipt moves into December.
words.whenToUse: Use it to compare plausible combinations of conditions before selecting an action.
words.avoidOrMisuse: A scenario is not automatically a forecast or a probability statement; specify the conditions it assumes.
words.mission: Describe one fictional scenario and the assumption that distinguishes it from the base case.

sales-business-development.meaning: A coherent possible situation used to explore how a proposal might perform under particular conditions.
sales-business-development.example: In the smaller-rollout scenario, the customer would start with two branches and review the remaining locations after the first month.
sales-business-development.whenToUse: Use when comparing plausible alternatives and helping a buyer or colleague prepare for different combinations of events.
sales-business-development.avoidOrMisuse: A scenario is not a prediction; state its assumptions and avoid implying every scenario has the same likelihood.
sales-business-development.mission: Describe two fictional purchasing scenarios and explain how each would change the order size, delivery timing, or proposed support.

operations-supply-chain.meaning: A coherent set of possible conditions used to explore how an operation might respond, not a prediction of what will happen.
operations-supply-chain.example: The lower-demand scenario assumes the promotion starts late, so the packing team can compare staffing needs with the original launch case.
operations-supply-chain.whenToUse: Use it when uncertain events could combine into different operating conditions and a single forecast conceals important choices.
operations-supply-chain.avoidOrMisuse: Label the assumptions and avoid assigning probability without support; a scenario can be useful even when its likelihood is unknown.
operations-supply-chain.mission: Compare two fictional promotion scenarios and identify how the staffing decision changes between them.

consulting-strategy.meaning: A coherent possible future situation used to explore implications for a decision under a stated combination of conditions.
consulting-strategy.example: In the higher-demand scenario, the central team reaches its capacity earlier, so the client would need to review the staffing approach before expansion.
consulting-strategy.whenToUse: Use when helping a client consider plausible combinations of future events and how different options might perform under them.
consulting-strategy.avoidOrMisuse: A scenario is not a forecast or a probability statement unless explicitly developed as one; make its assumptions and purpose clear.
consulting-strategy.mission: Describe two fictional scenarios for a service strategy and explain the practical difference each creates for the recommended option.

words.meaning: The span between stated lower and upper values or possible outcomes.
words.example: The current estimate is a range of £15,000 to £18,000, depending on the final delivery charge.
words.whenToUse: Use it to show uncertainty when one exact number would suggest more precision than you have.
words.avoidOrMisuse: A range is not a guarantee that the outcome cannot fall outside it; explain how its limits were chosen.
words.mission: Present a fictional cost range and state the main reason the amount is uncertain.

words.meaning: The remaining room before an available amount or agreed limit is used up.
words.example: The revised cash schedule shows £9,000 of headroom above the team's chosen planning buffer.
words.whenToUse: Use it to explain the remaining flexibility relative to a clearly defined resource or limit.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Name the limit and period; headroom does not have a single meaning across cash, budgets, and lending arrangements.
words.mission: Explain the remaining headroom in a fictional plan and state the limit used.

sales-business-development.meaning: Available capacity or flexibility before a stated limit is reached, such as delivery workload or an approved budget.
sales-business-development.example: The onboarding team has headroom for one additional customer this month, provided the current implementation finishes on the expected date.
sales-business-development.whenToUse: Use when explaining practical room to accommodate an order, discount, or change within a clearly identified constraint.
sales-business-development.avoidOrMisuse: Headroom needs a reference limit; avoid implying unused money or capacity is automatically available for any purpose.
sales-business-development.mission: Describe fictional delivery headroom and explain what you would confirm before offering the remaining implementation slot to a new customer.

words.meaning: When something happens and how that point relates to other events or periods.
words.example: The timing of the customer receipt matters because the supplier payment is due a week earlier.
words.whenToUse: Use it when the date of an event changes a period comparison or a cash discussion.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Calling a difference timing-related should not conceal a permanent change; explain when the effect is expected to reverse.
words.mission: Explain a fictional timing difference and identify the two dates that matter.

words.meaning: A specified event or condition that starts an agreed action or review.
words.example: A supplier delay of more than five working days is the agreed trigger for revisiting the delivery forecast.
words.whenToUse: Use it to make clear when a plan will be reviewed or a prepared action will begin.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Do not invent a trigger after an event and present it as previously agreed; identify the owner and agreed condition.
words.mission: Define a trigger for reviewing a fictional forecast and name who will respond.

words.meaning: To change an existing estimate, document, or plan in response to review or new information.
words.example: We will revise the forecast after operations confirms the new delivery schedule.
words.whenToUse: Use it when explaining what will change in an existing version and why.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Revising a forecast is different from rewriting the original approved comparison; keep both versions identifiable.
words.mission: Say when you will revise a fictional estimate and which new information will inform the change.

words.meaning: Information or records used to support or assess a statement or conclusion.
words.example: The dated completion note is supporting evidence for the service date stated in the report.
words.whenToUse: Use it when explaining the basis for a statement rather than asking a reader to accept it without support.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Evidence is usually uncountable: say two pieces of evidence, not two evidences. Consider relevance and reliability as well as quantity.
words.mission: Name the evidence supporting a fictional report statement and one limitation of that evidence.

words.meaning: To provide additional support for a statement through another relevant source or observation.
words.example: The customer's acknowledgement helps corroborate the service date shown in the completion record.
words.whenToUse: Use it when a second source strengthens an explanation or statement.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Two copies of the same unsupported statement do not provide independent corroboration; identify the additional source.
words.mission: Suggest a second source that could corroborate a fictional explanation.

operations-supply-chain.meaning: To provide additional supporting evidence for an account or finding, ideally from a relevant independent source.
operations-supply-chain.example: Warehouse receipt logs corroborate the arrival dates in the carrier report, although they do not establish when the supplier released each load.
operations-supply-chain.whenToUse: Use it when several records support the same operational detail but may answer different parts of the investigation.
operations-supply-chain.avoidOrMisuse: Agreement between copied records is not independent support; state which part of a claim is corroborated and what remains unverified.
operations-supply-chain.mission: Explain what fictional receipt logs corroborate about a delivery dispute and identify one question those logs cannot answer.

technology-engineering.meaning: To provide additional evidence that supports an existing claim, explanation, or finding.
technology-engineering.example: A second test with production-like account sizes would help corroborate the cache performance claim.
technology-engineering.whenToUse: Use it when a promising result needs support from another relevant observation or source of evidence.
technology-engineering.avoidOrMisuse: Do not treat repeating the same narrow benchmark unchanged as independent corroboration of performance for different workloads.
technology-engineering.mission: Propose a test that could corroborate the cache result for large accounts and explain why the evidence is additional.

people-human-resources.meaning: Support an account or interpretation with additional relevant information from another observation or appropriate source.
people-human-resources.example: A follow-up example may corroborate the candidate's explanation of how they coordinate work, though it will not establish consistency in every setting.
people-human-resources.whenToUse: Use when seeking additional support for an important interpretation rather than relying on one impression or isolated statement.
people-human-resources.avoidOrMisuse: Do not imply corroboration proves everything or authorise intrusive information gathering; use appropriate, relevant questions and established information channels.
people-human-resources.mission: Identify a fictional interview interpretation that needs more support and propose a relevant follow-up that could corroborate or challenge it.

healthcare.meaning: To provide additional evidence that supports a particular statement or part of an account.
healthcare.example: The email log can corroborate that a message was sent, but it does not show that the patient opened or understood it.
healthcare.whenToUse: Use it when another relevant record supports a narrowly stated communication fact rather than the entire surrounding account.
healthcare.avoidOrMisuse: Be explicit about the limit of the supporting evidence; duplicated records may not provide independent confirmation of an event.
healthcare.mission: State what a fictional email log corroborates and what still needs direct confirmation.

words.meaning: To check that information, a method, or an assumption is suitable and meets the intended requirements.
words.example: We will validate the report's assumptions against the delivery information confirmed by operations.
words.whenToUse: Use it when checking whether an input or approach is fit for a defined purpose.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Do not use validated to mean merely received or glanced at; explain what requirements were checked.
words.mission: Explain how you would validate one assumption in a fictional forecast.

sales-business-development.meaning: Check whether a claim, assumption, or proposed approach is adequately supported for the decision being considered.
sales-business-development.example: The trial will help validate whether shared reports reduce duplicate checking for this team, rather than proving the same benefit for every customer.
sales-business-development.whenToUse: Use when describing a structured check that could strengthen or weaken the basis for a commercial recommendation.
sales-business-development.avoidOrMisuse: Validate does not necessarily mean prove beyond doubt; specify what evidence would count and how narrow the conclusion would be.
sales-business-development.mission: Explain how a fictional pilot could validate one important proposal assumption, including what result would lead you to revise the offer.

consulting-strategy.meaning: Check whether a claim, assumption, or proposed approach has sufficient support for the purpose and decision being considered.
consulting-strategy.example: The trial can validate whether the new routing rule works for routine cases, but it will not establish suitability for every specialist enquiry.
consulting-strategy.whenToUse: Use when explaining what evidence a test should provide and how narrowly its conclusion can reasonably be applied.
consulting-strategy.avoidOrMisuse: Validate does not mean prove universally; specify the question, the evidence standard, and the circumstances the check does not cover.
consulting-strategy.mission: Explain how a fictional pilot would validate one decision-critical assumption, including the result that would lead you to revise the recommendation.

words.meaning: An item or result that falls outside a stated rule, expected pattern, or agreed condition.
words.example: The comparison produced one exception because a department used a different reporting date.
words.whenToUse: Use it to identify a result needing attention under a defined check or process.
words.avoidOrMisuse: An exception is not automatically an error or misconduct; explain the rule and investigate the reason.
words.mission: Describe an exception in a fictional report and state who will review it.

words.meaning: A specified level or boundary at which a different action or assessment begins.
words.example: The team agreed a £100 threshold for flagging differences in this internal comparison exercise.
words.whenToUse: Use it to explain the boundary that determines how a result will be handled.
words.avoidOrMisuse: A threshold belongs to a specified process; do not present an illustrative or internal value as a universal requirement.
words.mission: Describe a fictional review threshold and the action taken when it is exceeded.

sales-business-development.meaning: A defined level or condition at which a decision, action, or different treatment becomes relevant.
sales-business-development.example: We can discuss a volume discount once the order reaches the threshold stated in the approved pricing schedule.
sales-business-development.whenToUse: Use to make a decision rule explicit when an amount, level of evidence, or other condition changes what is possible.
sales-business-development.avoidOrMisuse: Do not invent an approval or discount threshold; distinguish a proposed decision point from an existing confirmed requirement.
sales-business-development.mission: Propose a fictional pilot success threshold for discussion and ask the customer whether it would provide enough evidence to consider a wider rollout.

consulting-strategy.meaning: A defined level or condition at which a decision, action, or change in approach becomes appropriate under an agreed rule.
consulting-strategy.example: The group should agree a threshold for acceptable repeat handling before the pilot starts, so the review does not redefine success after seeing the result.
consulting-strategy.whenToUse: Use when a recommendation needs an explicit decision point rather than a vague promise to proceed if things look good.
consulting-strategy.avoidOrMisuse: Do not invent a threshold or imply a proposed level is an established standard; explain its purpose and seek the relevant decision-maker's agreement.
consulting-strategy.mission: Suggest a fictional threshold for discussing pilot expansion and identify the client information needed to decide whether that level is appropriate.

words.meaning: The obligation to explain and take responsibility for an outcome or decision.
words.example: The team lead retains accountability for the close checklist even when individual checks are delegated.
words.whenToUse: Use it to clarify who must explain whether an agreed outcome was achieved.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Accountability is not simply blame after a failure; make expectations and authority clear beforehand.
words.mission: State who has accountability for a fictional reporting outcome and what they must confirm.

sales-business-development.meaning: Clear answerability for an outcome or decision, including the expectation to explain progress and address problems within one's remit.
sales-business-development.example: We need clear accountability for confirming the implementation scope so that sales and delivery do not each assume the other has checked it.
sales-business-development.whenToUse: Use when making ownership visible across teams and creating a reliable way to address unresolved commercial or delivery issues.
sales-business-development.avoidOrMisuse: Avoid equating accountability with blame; specify the outcome, the person's authority, and the information needed to fulfil the responsibility.
sales-business-development.mission: Clarify accountability for a fictional proposal handoff by naming the owned outcome, the responsible role, and the point at which progress will be reviewed.

operations-supply-chain.meaning: The clear obligation to answer for a decision or result and ensure agreed responsibilities receive appropriate follow-through.
operations-supply-chain.example: Accountability for the handover review will sit with the depot manager, who will report unresolved issues and confirm the next improvement actions.
operations-supply-chain.whenToUse: Use it when an improvement moves into normal operations and stakeholders need to know who will ensure it remains effective.
operations-supply-chain.avoidOrMisuse: Do not confuse accountability with a blame mechanism or scatter it across everyone; distinguish answerability from the tasks others contribute.
operations-supply-chain.mission: Assign fictional accountability for maintaining a depot handover process, including reporting and follow-through expectations.

people-human-resources.meaning: Clear answerability for a specified outcome or decision, including the expectation to explain progress and address issues within one's authority.
people-human-resources.example: Accountability for the induction schedule sits with the team lead, who needs the authority and information to coordinate contributions from other colleagues.
people-human-resources.whenToUse: Use when aligning responsibility with the ability to act and making it clear how progress or problems will be discussed.
people-human-resources.avoidOrMisuse: Do not use accountability as a synonym for blame or assign an outcome without considering the person's actual decision authority.
people-human-resources.mission: Explain fictional accountability for a team handoff, naming the owned outcome, the information needed, and the route for raising an unresolved dependency.

healthcare.meaning: An obligation to answer for an agreed responsibility or outcome and ensure appropriate follow-through.
healthcare.example: Accountability for keeping the handover directory current belongs with the service owner formally appointed through the organisation's approved process.
healthcare.whenToUse: Use it when a shared communication arrangement needs a clear person or role to ensure it remains maintained.
healthcare.avoidOrMisuse: Do not confuse accountability with blame or assign it without authority; distinguish the answerable role from contributors who carry out updates.
healthcare.mission: Explain fictional accountability for a communication directory, including the agreed review responsibility and how unresolved errors reach the authorised owner.

consulting-strategy.meaning: Clear answerability for an outcome or decision, including the expectation to report progress and address issues within an appropriate remit.
consulting-strategy.example: Accountability for improving the handoff sits with the service lead, who needs authority to agree the process and access the information used to review it.
consulting-strategy.whenToUse: Use when connecting ownership of a recommendation with the authority and information needed to implement it responsibly.
consulting-strategy.avoidOrMisuse: Do not use accountability as a synonym for blame or assign an outcome to someone who cannot influence the required decisions.
consulting-strategy.mission: Clarify fictional accountability for a strategic initiative by identifying the owned outcome, the required authority, and the progress information that will be reviewed.

words.meaning: Supervision or review of an activity to check that it is being carried out appropriately.
words.example: The controller provides oversight of the close process through a weekly review of open items.
words.whenToUse: Use it to explain how work is supervised without implying that the supervisor performs every task.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Oversight can also mean an accidental omission. Use provide oversight for supervision and an oversight for a missed item.
words.mission: Explain who provides oversight of a fictional process and what they review.

healthcare.meaning: Ongoing supervision or review that checks an activity is being managed appropriately and significant issues receive attention.
healthcare.example: Service oversight will review outdated-contact reports and confirm whether the directory owner has resolved them through the approved update process.
healthcare.whenToUse: Use it when explaining how leaders maintain visibility of communication quality without personally performing every operational task.
healthcare.avoidOrMisuse: Oversight here means supervision, not an accidental omission; it should not be used to imply clinical validation of a communication resource.
healthcare.mission: Propose fictional oversight of a handover-contact directory, naming the information reviewers need and the action unresolved issues should prompt.

words.meaning: To give the required permission for an action to proceed.
words.example: Only the designated manager can authorise the change under the team's approved process.
words.whenToUse: Use it when formal permission is distinct from preparing, recommending, or checking an action.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Do not imply that any manager can authorise any action; refer to the authority defined for the specific process.
words.mission: Ask who can authorise a fictional report change and what information they need.

words.meaning: To record information clearly so that another person can understand and review it later.
words.example: Please document the reason for the change and link the reviewer's response in the working file.
words.whenToUse: Use it when a decision, explanation, or process needs a clear and retrievable record.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Recording a decision does not prove it was correct or approved; distinguish the record from the judgement it describes.
words.mission: Say what you will document after a fictional review meeting and where the record will be kept.

words.meaning: To check whether a particular fact or detail agrees with reliable supporting information.
words.example: We will verify the delivery date against the signed receipt before updating the note.
words.whenToUse: Use it for checking a specified fact, amount, date, or record.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Verifying one detail does not validate every assumption or the whole report; state exactly what you checked.
words.mission: Explain how you would verify one date or amount in a fictional report.

words.meaning: To take corrective action to address a problem or weakness.
words.example: The team will remediate the filing weakness by assigning an owner and checking each completed handover.
words.whenToUse: Use it when discussing a corrective plan in a review or control discussion.
words.avoidOrMisuse: A promise to remediate is not evidence that the problem is fixed; describe the action and how completion will be checked.
words.mission: Propose an action to remediate a fictional process weakness and a way to check the result.

words.meaning: Open and clear about the relevant facts, reasoning, and limitations.
words.example: The update is transparent about the missing confirmation and the checks already completed.
words.whenToUse: Use it when clear disclosure of the relevant position helps readers understand and assess your work.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Transparent communication does not require sharing confidential information with an inappropriate audience.
words.mission: Write a transparent update that names both a completed check and a remaining limitation.

people-human-resources.meaning: Clear enough about relevant reasoning, information, and process that affected people can understand how a decision or conclusion was reached.
people-human-resources.example: A transparent explanation identifies the criteria used for the project assignment and clarifies which questions the manager can answer about the decision.
people-human-resources.whenToUse: Use when explaining a people process in understandable terms while respecting legitimate limits on sharing personal or sensitive information.
people-human-resources.avoidOrMisuse: Transparency does not require disclosing another person's confidential details; explain the process and your information limits without speculating.
people-human-resources.mission: Draft a fictional transparent explanation of a team assignment that describes the reasoning and acknowledges information you cannot appropriately discuss.

words.meaning: Confidence about a specified matter that is supported by relevant information or checks.
words.example: The reconciliation gives the team additional assurance about the agreement between these two reports.
words.whenToUse: Use it to explain what a completed check gives the team confidence about.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Formal assurance engagements have defined meanings; do not present an informal internal check as an external assurance conclusion.
words.mission: Explain what assurance a fictional check provides and what it does not cover.

operations-supply-chain.meaning: Confidence supported by appropriate evidence and review that specified arrangements or controls are working as intended.
operations-supply-chain.example: Operational assurance should come from documented transfer tests and review of exceptions rather than from the overflow depot's optimistic readiness statement.
operations-supply-chain.whenToUse: Use it when leadership needs a substantiated basis for relying on a process, control, or implementation claim.
operations-supply-chain.avoidOrMisuse: Assurance is not an absolute guarantee; say what evidence was reviewed, its scope, and what remains outside the check.
operations-supply-chain.mission: Explain what assurance you would seek before a fictional depot transfer, naming the evidence and one limit on the conclusion.

healthcare.meaning: Confidence grounded in appropriate evidence and review that specified arrangements are working as intended within a stated scope.
healthcare.example: Communication assurance should examine whether approved contact details are actually used and whether reported errors reach the responsible owner for correction.
healthcare.whenToUse: Use it when leadership asks what evidence supports reliance on a communication process or implementation claim.
healthcare.avoidOrMisuse: Assurance is not a guarantee of clinical safety or patient understanding; state the evidence reviewed and what lies outside that check.
healthcare.mission: Explain what assurance a fictional template-use review can provide and identify a separate question about patient understanding it cannot settle.

words.meaning: Not yet settled or given a satisfactory explanation or solution.
words.example: The difference remains unresolved because the team has not yet confirmed which delivery date is correct.
words.whenToUse: Use it when work has taken place but the central question still lacks a settled answer.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Unresolved does not mean no one has acted; describe the work completed and the specific question that remains.
words.mission: Report an unresolved issue, the checks completed, and the next question to answer.

words.meaning: To make a point, requirement, or explanation easier to understand and less ambiguous.
words.example: Let me clarify the request: we need the delivery dates, not a revised annual budget.
words.whenToUse: Use it when uncertainty about meaning could lead a colleague to take the wrong action.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Clarify is not a polite label for repeating the same unclear wording; identify and explain the ambiguous point.
words.mission: Write a sentence that uses clarify to correct a fictional misunderstanding about a report request.

healthcare.meaning: To make a statement, arrangement, or question clearer by resolving a specific uncertainty or ambiguity.
healthcare.example: Could the responsible clinician clarify who will explain the existing plan and where the patient's remaining questions should be recorded?
healthcare.whenToUse: Use it when unclear wording or responsibility prevents colleagues from knowing what the agreed communication process requires.
healthcare.avoidOrMisuse: Name the uncertainty rather than asking someone to 'clarify everything'; clarification does not authorise changing a clinical plan yourself.
healthcare.mission: Ask a precise clarification question about a fictional plan-explanation task, identifying the missing owner or communication arrangement.

words.meaning: A consequence or practical meaning that follows from a fact, proposal, or decision.
words.example: The immediate implication of the delay is that the receipts move into the following month's cash forecast.
words.whenToUse: Use it to move from describing a fact to explaining why the reader should care.
words.avoidOrMisuse: Separate a confirmed consequence from a possible implication; do not imply certainty when another assumption is involved.
words.mission: State a fictional finding and explain one implication for the team's plan.

words.meaning: The reasoning that explains why an action, choice, or approach makes sense.
words.example: The rationale for delaying the workshop is to avoid the team's busiest reporting week.
words.whenToUse: Use it when the reader needs the reasoning behind a recommendation or decision.
words.avoidOrMisuse: A rationale is more than a preferred outcome; connect the choice to evidence, constraints, or objectives.
words.mission: Explain the rationale for a fictional recommendation using one supporting fact.

project-product.meaning: The reasoning that explains why a decision, recommendation, or approach makes sense in its context.
project-product.example: The rationale for a limited pilot is to test repeat-work savings without exposing every customer to a new process.
project-product.whenToUse: Use it when stakeholders need to understand the logic connecting evidence, constraints, and your proposed action.
project-product.avoidOrMisuse: Do not use rationale as a polished label for a preference; make the supporting reasoning inspectable.
project-product.mission: Explain the rationale for starting with one segment and name the evidence that could change that choice.

sales-business-development.meaning: The connected reasons that explain why a particular decision, recommendation, or commercial approach makes sense.
sales-business-development.example: The rationale for a smaller pilot is to test the customer's most important workflow before either team commits to extensive configuration.
